hints: Start by sorting the four stages into two groups - which one can happen without any mitochondria at all, and which three need mitochondria?
For the mitochondrial stages, remember the mitochondrion has two very different working areas - a fluid centre where cycles happen and a folded membrane where electron carriers pump protons.
walkthrough:
Separate glycolysis from the rest**
Glycolysis does not need oxygen or mitochondria. Its enzymes are free in the fluid part of the cell, so in a muscle cell this is the cytoplasm, also called cytosol or sarcoplasm. Glucose is split to two pyruvate here.

Place the link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix**
Once pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, it is decarboxylated in the link reaction and then completely oxidised in the Krebs cycle. Both sets of soluble enzymes are in the mitochondrial matrix, the fluid centre enclosed by the inner membrane.

Place oxidative phosphorylation on the membrane**
The electron transport chain proteins and ATP synthase are built into the inner mitochondrial membrane, folded into cristae to give a large surface area. This is where the proton gradient is formed and ATP is made by chemiosmosis.
Final answer: glycolysis: cytoplasm / cytosol / sarcoplasm; link reaction: mitochondrial matrix; Krebs cycle: mitochondrial matrix; oxidative phosphorylation: inner mitochondrial membrane / cristae.

hints: Think about what the cell surface membrane lets through by simple diffusion - small non-polar molecules pass the phospholipid bilayer easily, but what happens with larger charged molecules?
Think about what adding a phosphate group does to glucose in terms of size, charge and polarity, and whether a membrane protein exists to carry that new molecule out.
walkthrough:
Recall how glucose normally crosses the membrane**
Glucose is polar, so it cannot pass directly through the hydrophobic phospholipid bilayer. It enters by facilitated diffusion through a specific glucose carrier or channel protein that fits its exact shape.

See why phosphorylation traps it**
Adding a phosphate makes the molecule bigger and more polar and charged. It no longer fits the glucose transport protein, and there is no transport protein for phosphorylated glucose. The phospholipid bilayer is impermeable to large polar molecules, so it is trapped inside the cell for glycolysis.
Final answer: Phosphorylated glucose is too large to pass through the membrane / channel and is polar / charged, and there is no specific carrier / channel protein for it, so it cannot diffuse out.

hints: Start by listing which stages of aerobic respiration can still run when oxygen is missing and which stages must stop.
Recall how much net ATP comes directly from glycolysis alone and what type of phosphorylation this is.
Think about what happens to pyruvate when it cannot enter the link reaction and Krebs cycle in animal muscle.
Consider the role of oxygen at the end of the electron transport chain and what happens to that chain without it.
Link where most aerobic ATP normally comes from to why stopping that stage causes such a large drop in yield.
walkthrough:
Only glycolysis can continue**
Without oxygen, pyruvate cannot be oxidised in the link reaction and Krebs cycle. Only the conversion of glucose to pyruvate in glycolysis in the cytoplasm continues.

Small ATP yield by substrate-linked phosphorylation**
Glycolysis gives a net of only 2 ATP per glucose, made directly by transfer of phosphate from a substrate to ADP. This is substrate-linked phosphorylation. No additional ATP is made this way in the Krebs cycle because the Krebs cycle has stopped.

Pyruvate to lactate wastes energy**
In muscle, pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD for glycolysis to continue. Lactate is still energy-rich because glucose has not been fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, so much chemical energy remains locked in lactate.

No final electron acceptor**
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain. Without it, electrons cannot flow along the carriers, no proton gradient is built up, and chemiosmosis stops.

Loss of the main ATP source**
In aerobic conditions most ATP, about 28-34 per glucose, is made by oxidative phosphorylation using the electron transport chain and ATP synthase. Because this whole system stops in anaerobic conditions, total yield falls from about 30-32 ATP to only 2 ATP.

Final answer: In anaerobic conditions only glycolysis occurs giving a net of 2 ATP by substrate-linked phosphorylation only. Pyruvate is reduced to lactate which still contains much energy. Oxygen is absent as the final electron acceptor so the electron transport chain / chemiosmosis / oxidative phosphorylation stops, and this is where most aerobic ATP is made.

hints: Think about what has built up in the blood and muscles during anaerobic exercise that now needs oxygen to be removed.
Recall where in the body lactate is processed after exercise and what it is converted back into.
Think about what else needs refilling with oxygen besides removing lactate, such as oxygen stores in blood and muscle and the still-high rate of ATP use.
walkthrough:
Repay the oxygen debt**
During anaerobic work the body built up lactate without using oxygen. After exercise, extra oxygen is taken in to reverse those anaerobic effects. This is called the oxygen debt.

Remove lactate in the liver**
Lactate is carried in blood to liver cells where oxygen is used in aerobic respiration to provide ATP to convert lactate back to pyruvate and then to glucose. This removes lactate from blood and muscle.

Restore oxygen stores and meet continued demand**
Extra oxygen re-oxygenates haemoglobin in blood and myoglobin in muscle that gave up oxygen during exercise. Breathing also stays high because heart rate, ion pumping and other metabolic processes are still using extra ATP for a short time after stopping.

Final answer: Extra oxygen repays the oxygen debt. It is used to oxidise / convert lactate to pyruvate / glucose in the liver, to re-oxygenate haemoglobin and myoglobin, and to supply ATP while metabolic rate remains high.
